SOURCE OF FACTS: the component names, durations, mark totals, weightings, exercise descriptions, assessment objectives and grading on these pages were read from the official Cambridge International syllabus for 0510 covering examinations in 2027, 2028 and 2029 (document 721337). Where a page states a figure, that is where it came from. The 2024-2026 syllabus differs and is described as a separate arrangement, never blended with the new one. Nothing here reproduces Cambridge text, question papers or mark schemes. All practice material is original RCF English work and is labelled as such on every page that carries it.

pages.description: Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language (0510, 0511, 0991, 0993): the three components, their durations, marks and assessment objectives, explained in full.
pages.keywords: IGCSE English as a Second Language, Cambridge IGCSE ESL 0510, 0511, 0991, 0993, IGCSE ESL papers, IGCSE ESL syllabus, IGCSE English second language revision

hero.text: Three components, six written exercises, five listening exercises and a recorded speaking test. This guide takes each of them apart, states where every figure comes from, and gives you original practice with answers.

blocks.text: **Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language is assessed by three components: a two-hour Reading and Writing paper worth 70%, a listening paper of about fifty minutes worth 30%, and a speaking test of ten to fifteen minutes.** Whether the speaking mark counts towards your grade depends on which of the four syllabus codes your school entered you for.

blocks.title: Which syllabus this page describes
text: The component structure, durations, marks, weightings and exercise descriptions below are taken from the **Cambridge International syllabus for 0510, English as a Second Language (Speaking Endorsement), for examinations in 2027, 2028 and 2029**.

**If you are sitting in 2026, you are on the earlier 2024-2026 syllabus, and the Listening and Speaking components are not the same.** Cambridge changed the Listening paper to entirely multiple-choice questions and raised the Speaking component to 40 marks for 2027. Check the syllabus for your own examination year on the [Cambridge 0510 page](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/programmes-and-qualifications/cambridge-igcse-english-second-language-oral-endorsement-0510/) before relying on any figure.
Cambridge states that examinations are available in the June and November series, and also in the March series in India.

blocks.heading: The four syllabus codes, and which one is yours
text: Cambridge offers this subject under four codes. They teach the same content and use the same written papers. Two things separate them: what happens to the speaking mark, and which grade scale is used.

blocks.heading: 0510, 0511, 0991 and 0993 compared
blocks.caption: The speaking arrangement and grade scale are the only differences. The taught content is the same.
rows: IGCSE English as a Second Language (Speaking Endorsement)
Reported separately, graded 1 (high) to 5 (low). Does not count towards the written grade.
IGCSE English as a Second Language (Count-in Speaking)
IGCSE (9-1) English as a Second Language (Count-in Speaking)
IGCSE (9-1) English as a Second Language (Speaking Endorsement)

blocks.title: There are no longer Core and Extended tiers
text: Cambridge removed tiering from this subject with the 2024 syllabus. Every candidate now sits the same papers and is eligible for the full grade range. If you are using a revision book or a website that talks about choosing between a Core paper and an Extended paper for English as a Second Language, it is describing an arrangement that no longer exists.

blocks.heading: Assessment overview: the three components
blocks.caption: From the Cambridge 0510 syllabus for examinations in 2027, 2028 and 2029. All candidates take all three components.
rows: Approximately 50 minutes, including 6 minutes to transfer answers
Separately endorsed for 0510 and 0993; counts towards the grade for 0511 and 0991

parts.heading: Component 1: Reading and Writing, 2 hours, 60 marks
text: Six exercises: four reading and two writing. You answer every question. The reading exercises use text types such as articles, blogs and reports, and mix multiple-choice, matching and short written answers. Both writing exercises ask for 120 to 160 words of continuous prose, and both carry 15 marks split as 6 for content and 9 for language.

The first writing exercise is informal - an email to a friend or relative. The second is formal or semi-formal, and may be an article, a report, an essay or a review. Answers are written on the question paper. Dictionaries may not be used.
[Open the exercise-by-exercise guide to this paper](global-english/igcse/english-as-a-second-language/reading-and-writing/).

parts.heading: Component 2: Listening, about 50 minutes, 40 marks
text: For 2027 onwards this paper is five exercises and 40 questions, and every question is multiple choice. You hear each recording twice. At the end you have six minutes to transfer your answers to a separate answer sheet, and that transfer time is included in the fifty minutes.

The five exercises move from short extracts with picture options, through paired questions on short extracts and sentence completion from a monologue, to a matching task across six short monologues and finally eight questions on an interview.

parts.heading: Component 3: Speaking, 10 to 15 minutes, 40 marks
text: Conducted and marked by your own teacher, recorded in full, and moderated by Cambridge. There are five stages: an introduction and a warm-up, neither of which is assessed, then an interview, a short talk prepared from a card in one minute, and a discussion of the same topic. Only the last three are assessed.
[Open the speaking test guide](global-english/igcse/english-as-a-second-language/speaking-test/).

blocks.heading: Assessment objectives and their weightings
blocks.caption: Approximate weightings for the qualification, from the Cambridge 0510 syllabus for 2027-2029. Descriptions here are summarised, not quoted.
rows: Understanding stated facts; following ideas, opinions and attitudes across a text; selecting detail for a purpose; understanding what is implied
Communicating information, ideas and opinions; organising with linking devices; range and accuracy of grammar and vocabulary; register and style for the purpose and audience
Understanding specific information, speakers' ideas and attitudes, connections between them, and what is implied
Communicating ideas, facts and opinions; range and control of vocabulary and structures; developing responses and maintaining communication; pronunciation and intonation

blocks.title: How the objectives sit inside each component
text: Component 1 is half reading and half writing. Component 2 is entirely listening. Component 3 is entirely speaking. There is no overlap, which is useful for revision: a weak reading mark can only be repaired in Component 1, and no amount of listening practice will move it.

blocks.heading: Questions about Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language

items.q: How long is the Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language exam?
a: For the 2027-2029 syllabus, the Reading and Writing paper is 2 hours, the Listening paper is approximately 50 minutes including six minutes to transfer answers, and the Speaking test is approximately 10 to 15 minutes. That is about three hours of assessment in total, taken on separate occasions.

items.q: How many marks is IGCSE ESL out of?
a: The Reading and Writing paper carries 60 marks and is worth 70% of the qualification. The Listening paper carries 40 marks and is worth 30%. The Speaking test carries 40 marks; for 0510 and 0993 these are reported separately on the certificate, and for 0511 and 0991 they count towards the grade.

items.q: How many words should I write for IGCSE ESL writing?
a: Both writing exercises ask for 120 to 160 words. Writing far under that range makes it difficult to develop the prompts and costs content marks; writing far over it usually costs accuracy rather than earning credit. Plan for about 140 words and cover every prompt.

items.q: Is IGCSE English as a Second Language still Core and Extended?
a: No. Cambridge removed tiering from this subject with the 2024 syllabus. All candidates now take the same papers and are eligible for the full range of grades.

items.q: Can I use a dictionary in the exam?
a: No. The Cambridge syllabus states that dictionaries may not be used in the Reading and Writing paper or in the Speaking test.

items.q: Do I hear the listening recordings more than once?
a: Yes. Candidates hear each recorded text twice. Use the first listening to understand the situation and the second to confirm the specific answers rather than trying to settle every question on the first pass.

pages.title: IGCSE ESL Reading and Writing Paper
pages.metaTitle: IGCSE ESL Reading and Writing Paper: All Six Exercises Explained | RCF English
pages.description: What each of the six exercises in the IGCSE ESL Reading and Writing paper asks, the marks it carries, and how to spend the two hours.
pages.keywords: IGCSE ESL reading and writing, IGCSE English question types, how to answer IGCSE English questions, Cambridge IGCSE 0510 paper 1, IGCSE ESL exercise 3 notes, IGCSE ESL multiple matching

hero.text: Two hours, six exercises, sixty marks. Thirty of those marks are reading and thirty are writing, and most lost marks come from mistaking which kind of answer an exercise wants.

blocks.text: **The Reading and Writing paper has six exercises: four reading worth 30 marks in total, and two writing worth 15 marks each.** Exercises 1 to 4 test whether you can find, follow, select and infer. Exercises 5 and 6 test whether you can write 120 to 160 words in the right register for a stated purpose and audience.

blocks.heading: The six exercises at a glance
blocks.caption: From the Cambridge 0510 syllabus for examinations in 2027, 2028 and 2029.
rows: Read one text and answer six questions with short answers. The first five need one answer each; the last needs three.
Multiple matching. Read one text in up to five sections, or up to five short related texts, and match nine questions to the right one.
Read a text and complete a set of brief notes.
Read a text and answer six multiple-choice questions with three options each.
Write an informal email of 120-160 words.
Write a formal or semi-formal article, report, essay or review of 120-160 words.

blocks.heading: How to spend the two hours

items.title: Reading exercises 1 to 4: about 55 minutes
text: Thirty marks in under an hour. That is roughly two minutes a mark, which is comfortable if you do not re-read whole texts. Read the questions before the text for Exercises 1 and 3, so you know what you are hunting for.

items.title: Exercise 5, the informal email: about 25 minutes
text: Five minutes planning against the prompts, fifteen writing, five checking. The plan is what protects your content mark.

items.title: Exercise 6, the formal task: about 30 minutes
text: Slightly longer, because the register is harder to hold and the format has to be right. Decide in the first minute whether you are writing an article, a report, an essay or a review - the rubric tells you.

items.title: Final check: about 10 minutes
text: Check the two writing answers only. Read for verb tenses, for plural agreement and for whether every prompt has actually been answered. Do not spend this time changing reading answers on a feeling.

parts.heading: Exercise 1: short answers, 8 marks
text: The text is likely to contain facts, opinions, ideas and attitudes. Five questions want a single answer; the sixth wants three separate ones and is worth three marks.
bullets: Answer in a word or a short phrase. Full sentences waste time and cannot earn extra credit.
When a question asks for three things, give exactly three. A fourth answer that is wrong can cancel a right one.
Copy names, numbers and spellings exactly from the text.

parts.heading: Exercise 2: multiple matching, 9 marks
text: Nine questions, one mark each, matched against sections of one text or against several short related texts. This exercise rewards skimming, not close reading.
bullets: Read all nine questions first and underline the idea in each - not the whole question.
Expect the wording in the text to differ from the wording in the question. The test is whether you recognise the same idea in different words.
A section can be the answer to more than one question unless the paper says otherwise, so do not eliminate a section simply because you have used it.

parts.heading: Exercise 3: note-making, 7 marks
text: You complete a set of brief notes under headings the paper provides. Each response is worth one mark.
bullets: Notes, not sentences. A short phrase lifted accurately from the text is the ideal answer.
The headings tell you the category. If a heading says *Equipment needed*, a note about cost earns nothing however true it is.
Do not put two ideas on one line hoping one of them is right. Choose.

parts.heading: Exercise 4: multiple choice, 6 marks
text: Six questions with three options, A, B or C. Questions may be about main ideas, about details, or about the attitudes and opinions expressed. You write the letter.
bullets: Find the part of the text the question refers to before you look at the options. Reading the options first makes all three sound plausible.
Wrong options are usually true statements that do not answer the question, or half-true statements with one word changed.
Never leave a letter blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer.

parts.heading: Exercises 5 and 6: the writing, 15 marks each
text: Both are 120 to 160 words. Both are marked out of 6 for content and 9 for language. The stimulus tells you the purpose, the format and the audience, and those three things decide almost everything about your answer.

Content marks come from addressing every prompt **and developing it**. A candidate who mentions all the prompts in one sentence each has answered the task without developing it, and stops around half marks. Language marks come from range, accuracy and organisation together - a very safe answer with no errors does not reach the top band on range.

blocks.heading: In the writing exercises
do: Plan against the prompts: one line of notes for each, so none is forgotten.
Develop two of the prompts properly rather than listing all of them thinly.
Match the register the rubric asks for - informal for Exercise 5, formal or semi-formal for Exercise 6.
Use paragraphs. Three or four short paragraphs read far better than one block.
Count the words once, at the end, and stop within range.
dont: Do not open a formal task with *Hi* or close it with *See you soon*.
Do not learn an essay by heart and bend the task to fit it - content marks are for this task.
Do not use text-message spellings even in the informal email.
Do not write 300 words to be safe. Accuracy falls and the extra earns nothing.
Do not leave the format unmarked: a report needs headings, a review needs an opinion, an article needs a title.

blocks.title: Original RCF practice
text: The [RCF Model Paper 1](global-english/igcse/english-as-a-second-language/papers/rcf-model-paper-1/) is a full original paper in this format, with a [marking guide](global-english/igcse/english-as-a-second-language/papers/rcf-model-paper-1-mark-scheme/). It is unofficial practice material written by RCF English, not a Cambridge paper.

blocks.heading: Questions about the Reading and Writing paper

items.q: How many marks is the IGCSE ESL Reading and Writing paper?
a: Sixty marks, and it is worth 70% of the qualification. The four reading exercises carry 8, 9, 7 and 6 marks, making 30; the two writing exercises carry 15 marks each, making 30.

items.q: Do I write in full sentences in the reading exercises?
a: No. Exercises 1 and 3 want short answers - a word or a phrase. Exercise 3 in particular asks for brief notes, so a phrase copied accurately from the text is what earns the mark. Full sentences take time you need for the writing exercises and cannot earn more credit.

items.q: What happens if I write more than 160 words?
a: There is no automatic penalty for length, but longer answers tend to lose language marks through hurried accuracy and to drift away from the prompts. The range of 120 to 160 words is the length in which the task can be completed well, which is why it is set.

items.q: Is Exercise 6 always an essay?
a: No. The Cambridge syllabus describes Exercise 6 as a formal or semi-formal response that may be an article, a report, an essay or a review. The rubric on the paper tells you which one, along with the purpose and the audience, so read it before you plan.

pages.metaTitle: IGCSE English Writing Formats: Email, Article, Report, Review, Essay | RCF English
pages.description: Informal email, article, report, review and essay for IGCSE ESL: the shape each one needs, model openings, and original practice tasks.

hero.text: Five formats, one paper. The rubric names the format, the purpose and the audience, and getting those three right is worth more than any phrase you have memorised.

blocks.text: **Exercise 5 is always an informal email. Exercise 6 is formal or semi-formal, and may be an article, a report, an essay or a review.** Each format has a shape an examiner expects to see, and the shape takes about thirty seconds to plan once you know it.

blocks.heading: The five formats compared
blocks.caption: All five are written in 120-160 words and marked out of 6 for content and 9 for language.
rows: Greeting, reason for writing, two developed points, sign-off
Asking the reader a question back
Title, hook, two developed points, closing thought
A title and a direct appeal to the reader
Title, purpose, findings under headings, recommendation
Sub-headings and a recommendation at the end
What it is, what was good, what was less good, recommendation
A clear verdict, not just description
Introduction, argument for, argument against, conclusion
Discourse markers and a stated opinion at the end

parts.heading: The informal email (Exercise 5)
text: Written to a friend or a relative. The examiner is looking for natural warmth, not slang. Contractions are correct here; so are direct questions and short exclamations.
bullets: Open with a greeting and a line of contact: *Hi Sara, thanks for your message - sorry it has taken me so long to reply.*
Say why you are writing before you say anything else.
Develop two prompts fully rather than four thinly.
Close by turning back to the reader: *Let me know what you think. Write soon!*

parts.heading: The article
text: Written for a school magazine, a website or a newsletter. It has readers, and it should sound aware of them.
bullets: Give it a title. An article without a title looks like an essay and loses the format mark.
Open with a hook - a question, a surprising fact, or a short scene.
Address the reader at least once: *You have probably noticed this yourself.*
Finish with a thought rather than a summary.

parts.heading: The report
text: Written for someone with authority to act - a head teacher, a manager, a committee. Its job is to inform and then to recommend.
bullets: Give it a title, then state its purpose in the first line: *This report examines...*
Use two or three short sub-headings. They are the clearest signal of the format.
Keep the tone neutral. A report describes; it does not complain.
End with a recommendation, clearly labelled.

parts.heading: The review
text: Written about something you experienced - a film, a book, a restaurant, an event - for readers deciding whether to try it themselves.
bullets: Name the thing and the occasion in the first sentence.
Balance it: something that worked and something that did not. A review that only praises reads as an advertisement.
Justify each judgement with one specific detail.
End with a recommendation and who it suits.

parts.heading: The essay
text: Written to discuss a statement or a question, usually for a teacher. It is the most formal of the five.
bullets: Introduce the issue in one sentence without repeating the question word for word.
One paragraph for each side, each with a reason and an example.
Use linking words to show the turn: *However*, *On the other hand*, *Nevertheless*.
State your own view in the conclusion, and only there.

items.label: Informal email - opening
items.prompt: A friend has asked what your new school is like. Write an email of 120-160 words. (Original RCF practice task, in the style of Exercise 5.)
sample: Hi Nadia,
Thanks for your message! Sorry I have taken a week to reply - the first days at a new school are busier than I expected.
You asked what it is like here. Honestly, the building took some getting used to...
notes: The greeting and the apology establish an informal register immediately.
*You asked what it is like here* answers the prompt directly instead of drifting.
The contracted forms and the exclamation mark are appropriate here and would be wrong in Exercise 6.

items.label: Report - opening
items.prompt: Your head teacher has asked for a report on the school library. Write 120-160 words. (Original RCF practice task, in the style of Exercise 6.)
sample: **Report on the school library**
This report examines how the library is currently used and recommends two improvements.
**Current use**
The library is busiest between four and five o'clock, when almost every seat is taken...
notes: The title and the opening sentence name the format and the purpose in the first eleven words.
The sub-heading is the single clearest signal that this is a report and not an essay.
The tone is neutral: it describes the pressure on seats rather than complaining about it.

blocks.heading: Practice: five original RCF tasks
text: Each is written in the style of the examination by RCF English. They are not Cambridge questions. Write 120-160 words for each and check against the [model answers](global-english/igcse/english-as-a-second-language/model-answers/).
items: **Informal email.** A cousin is visiting your town next month and has asked what to bring and what to see. Write an email replying.
**Article.** Your school magazine is running a series called *One change I would make*. Write an article about one change you would make to the school day.
**Report.** Students have complained that the canteen queue is too slow. Write a report for the head teacher describing the problem and recommending two changes.
**Review.** Write a review of a film or a book you finished recently for the school website, saying who would enjoy it and who would not.
**Essay.** *Every student should learn to cook before leaving school.* Write an essay discussing this statement and giving your own opinion.

items.q: What writing formats come up in IGCSE English as a Second Language?
a: Exercise 5 is an informal email. Exercise 6 is a formal or semi-formal response, which the Cambridge syllabus describes as an article, a report, an essay or a review. The rubric on the paper tells you which one is required, together with the purpose and audience.

items.q: How do I know whether to write formally or informally?
a: The audience in the rubric decides it. A friend, a cousin or a classmate means informal. A head teacher, a manager, an organiser, a magazine's readers or an examiner means formal or semi-formal. If the rubric names a format such as report or essay, that is formal regardless of who reads it.

items.q: Should I use sub-headings in a report?
a: Yes. Two or three short sub-headings are the clearest way to show that you have understood the format, and they help you organise the content marks. Do not use them in an essay or an email.

items.q: Do I need a title for an article?
a: Yes. An article without a title reads as an essay, and format is part of the content mark. One short title line is enough, and it counts towards your word total.

hero.text: Two answers to the same task: one that would reach the top band, and one that would sit in the middle. The difference between them is easier to see than to describe.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Every task and every answer on this page was written by RCF English. They are **not** Cambridge questions, not real examination answers, and not taken from any mark scheme.

Cambridge publishes its own specimen answers and examiner reports through the [Cambridge 0510 past papers page](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/programmes-and-qualifications/cambridge-igcse-english-second-language-oral-endorsement-0510/past-papers/) and the School Support Hub. Use both: the official material shows you the standard, and these answers show you the reasoning.

blocks.text: **Writing is marked out of 15: six marks for content and nine for language.** Content is task fulfilment and the development of ideas. Language is range, accuracy and organisation. Almost every answer that stalls in the middle does so for the same reason - it mentions the prompts without developing them.

items.label: Task
items.prompt: Your cousin is visiting your town next month and has written to ask what to bring, what to see, and whether they will need much money. Write an email of 120-160 words replying. (Original RCF practice task.)
sample: This is the task both answers below respond to.

items.label: Answer A - the standard to aim for
sample: Hi Danesh,
It was so good to hear that you are finally coming! I have been telling everyone here that my cousin is visiting.

About what to bring: pack light clothes, but not only light clothes. It is warm all day, and then the evenings by the river turn surprisingly cold, so bring one jacket you do not mind carrying around. Also bring proper shoes, because the old town is all steps.
For seeing things, give me one whole Saturday. The market only opens properly at the weekend and it is the one thing you should not miss - it takes over three streets and smells of grilled corn.
Money you will hardly need. Buses are almost free, and my mother has already announced that you are eating at our house every evening.
Tell me your arrival time and I will meet you.
See you soon!
notes: **Content, high band.** All three prompts are answered, and two of them are genuinely developed - the clothes advice has a reason attached, and the market has a specific detail.
**Language, high band.** The range is wide: *I do not mind carrying around*, *turn surprisingly cold*, *has already announced*. The organisation moves prompt by prompt with clear paragraphs.
**Register.** Warm and natural throughout, and it turns back to the reader at the end, which is what an email does and an essay does not.
The specific detail - *smells of grilled corn* - is what separates this from a competent answer. It costs four words.

items.label: Answer B - a middle-band answer, and why it stops there
sample: Hi Danesh,
Thank you for your email. I am very happy that you are coming to my town next month. It will be very nice to see you again after a long time.
You asked me what you should bring. I think you should bring clothes and shoes. The weather here is very hot so bring light clothes.
You also asked what to see. There are many interesting places in my town. There is a market, a museum and a park. I am sure you will like them very much.
You asked about money. Do not worry about money. It is not very expensive here.
I am waiting for you. Please tell me when you are coming.
Best wishes,
Arun
notes: **Content, middle band.** Every prompt is mentioned, and none is developed. *There is a market, a museum and a park* is a list, not an answer - it tells the reader nothing they could act on.

**Language, middle band.** The English is accurate, and that is exactly the trap: accuracy alone does not reach the top band, because range is marked too. The sentences are short and similar in shape.

**What would move it up.** Choose one place instead of three and say something true about it. Give the clothing advice a reason. The word count is already there - the words are simply being spent on *very nice*, *very much*, *very hot*.
**Register note.** *Best wishes* is a formal sign-off borrowed from a letter. In an email to a cousin it is slightly off.

items.label: Task
items.prompt: Students have complained that the canteen queue at your school is too slow. Your head teacher has asked you to write a report describing the problem and recommending two changes. Write 120-160 words. (Original RCF practice task.)
sample: This is the task the answer below responds to.

items.label: Answer - the standard to aim for
sample: **Report on the canteen queue**
This report describes why the canteen queue has become slow and recommends two changes.
**The problem**

The queue is longest between 12.30 and 12.50, when all three year groups break together. Because there is a single serving point, students who want only a drink wait behind students buying a full meal. Several students told me they now skip lunch rather than lose most of the break standing in line.
**Recommendations**

First, a second serving point could be opened for drinks and snacks only, which would remove roughly half the queue. Second, the three year groups could break ten minutes apart, spreading the same number of students across a longer period.
Neither change requires new equipment, and both could be trialled for a fortnight before a decision is taken.
notes: **Format.** Title, statement of purpose, two sub-headings, recommendations at the end. An examiner can see the format from across the room.
**Content, high band.** The problem is given a cause, not just a description, and each recommendation is followed by its effect.
**Language, high band.** Formal and neutral: *Several students told me*, not *everyone is angry*. The conditional forms - *could be opened*, *would remove* - are exactly right for a recommendation.
**The closing line does real work.** Offering a trial shows awareness of the reader, who has to decide.
Notice what is absent: no contractions, no exclamation marks, no direct address to the reader. That is the difference from Exercise 5.

blocks.heading: Mark your own writing honestly
text: Work through these before you look at a model answer. Most of the marks lost in this paper are found by the fourth question.
items: Have I answered **every** prompt in the rubric?
Have I developed at least two of them with a reason or an example?
Is the format visible - title, sub-headings, greeting, sign-off - as the task requires?
Is the register right for the audience named in the rubric?
Have I used more than one sentence shape, or is every sentence subject-verb-object?
Have I checked verb tenses and plural agreement specifically?

items.q: Are these real IGCSE examination answers?
a: No. Every task and answer on this page was written by RCF English as practice material in the style of the examination. Cambridge's own specimen answers and examiner reports are published through its past papers page and the School Support Hub, and are the authoritative guide to the standard.

items.q: Why does an accurate answer only get middle marks?
a: Because language is marked on range, accuracy and organisation together, and content is marked on development as well as coverage. An answer with no grammatical errors but short, repetitive sentences and undeveloped ideas has met one of those criteria and not the others. Adding one developed example usually moves an answer more than correcting one article would.

items.q: Can I memorise a model answer and adapt it in the exam?
a: It rarely works. Content marks are awarded for answering this task and developing these prompts, so a pre-learned answer usually reads as off-topic and caps the content mark. Learning the shape of each format is worth doing; learning the sentences is not.

pages.title: IGCSE ESL Speaking Test
pages.metaTitle: IGCSE English Speaking Test: Structure, Topics and Marks | RCF English
pages.description: The Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language speaking test explained: the five stages, how long each lasts, which parts are assessed, the topics that come up, and original RCF practice cards.
pages.keywords: IGCSE English speaking topics, IGCSE ESL speaking test, Cambridge IGCSE speaking exam, IGCSE speaking short talk, IGCSE speaking test marks

hero.text: Ten to fifteen minutes with your own teacher, recorded from start to finish. Two of the five stages are not assessed at all, which surprises most candidates.

blocks.text: **The speaking test is conducted and marked by your own teacher, recorded in full, and moderated by Cambridge.** It carries 40 marks. For syllabuses 0510 and 0993 those marks are reported separately on your certificate, graded 1 (high) to 5 (low), and do not affect your written grade. For 0511 and 0991 they count towards the overall grade.

blocks.heading: The five stages
blocks.caption: From the Cambridge 0510 syllabus for examinations in 2027, 2028 and 2029. The whole test runs 10-15 minutes and is recorded from the introduction onwards.
rows: The teacher starts the recording and states the names, the candidate number and the date.
A short settling conversation using set questions.
The teacher introduces the topic and asks questions about it.
About 3-4 minutes, including 1 minute to prepare
You read an assessment card, prepare for up to a minute, then talk on your own about the topic.
A discussion of the same topic, led by the teacher's questions.

blocks.title: Two things worth knowing before the day
text: **You may not make written notes during the preparation minute.** The card stays with you until the end of the short talk, so use the minute to decide on two or three points and to fix an opening sentence in your head, not to draft.
**Dictionaries may not be used**, and the test is conducted entirely in English. The warm-up is genuinely there to settle you: nothing you say in it is marked.

blocks.heading: What the marks are actually for
text: The speaking assessment objectives cover four things: communicating a range of ideas, facts and opinions; showing control of a range of vocabulary and grammatical structures; developing responses and keeping the conversation going; and controlling pronunciation and intonation.

parts.heading: Development is the one that decides most marks
text: A short answer is rarely wrong. It is simply not enough to show what you can do. The single most useful habit is to answer, then extend without being asked.
bullets: **Weak:** *Yes, I like sport.*
**Better:** *Yes, I like sport - mainly badminton. I started because my sister played, and now I go three evenings a week. It is the only part of the day when I am not thinking about school.*
The second answer is the same opinion. What earns the marks is the reason, the history and the personal detail attached to it.

parts.heading: Pronunciation is about being followed, not about an accent
text: The objective is control of pronunciation and intonation, not sounding like a particular country. Speaking a little more slowly than feels natural, and letting your voice rise and fall rather than staying flat, does more for this mark than any individual sound.

blocks.heading: Phrases that buy you thinking time

items.definition: Buys two seconds and sounds engaged rather than stalling.
items.example: Use it once, not four times.

items.term: I had not thought about it that way before, but...
items.definition: Signals that you are about to develop an idea rather than repeat one.
items.example: Useful in Part 3, where the teacher may challenge you.

items.definition: Opens a balanced answer, which shows range.
items.example: *It depends, really. At home I would say yes, but at school it is different because...*

items.definition: Asking for clarification is not a loss of marks. Maintaining communication is one of the objectives.
items.example: Far better than answering a question you did not understand.

blocks.heading: Original RCF practice cards
text: Five practice topics written by RCF English in the style of the assessment cards. They are not Cambridge cards. Give yourself one minute to prepare and then speak for three minutes without stopping.
items: **Learning outside the classroom.** Talk about something useful you have learned that was not taught at school - who taught you, how, and whether school could teach it.
**Living in a city or in a village.** Talk about where you would choose to live at twenty-five years old, and what you would miss about the other.
**Mobile telephones at school.** Talk about whether students should be able to keep their telephones with them during the school day.
**A meal you remember.** Talk about a meal that mattered - what it was, who was there, and why you still remember it.
**Doing one thing well.** Talk about whether it is better to be good at many things or excellent at one.

blocks.heading: On the day
do: Answer, then add a reason, then add an example. Three sentences, every time.
Use the preparation minute to choose two points and an opening sentence.
Ask for a question to be repeated if you did not follow it.
Let your voice move. A flat delivery makes good English sound uncertain.
Keep going in Part 2 even if you run out of your planned points - describe, compare, or say what you would change.
dont: Do not recite a memorised speech. The discussion in Part 3 will expose it immediately.
Do not answer *yes* or *no* and wait.
Do not apologise for your English. It uses up assessed time.
Do not try to use difficult vocabulary you are unsure of at the expense of being understood.
Do not treat the warm-up as the test - and do not treat it as unimportant either, because it settles your voice.

items.q: How long is the IGCSE ESL speaking test?
a: Approximately 10 to 15 minutes in total, from the beginning of the introduction to the end of Part 3, and the whole of it is recorded. Within that, the assessed parts are the interview, the short talk and the discussion.

items.q: What topics come up in the IGCSE speaking test?
a: Cambridge supplies the assessment cards, and your teacher selects one for you, so the exact topics are not published in advance. They are everyday, general topics that any candidate can discuss from experience - school life, free time, technology, food, travel, work and study choices, and questions about how things could be improved. You are never expected to have specialist knowledge.

items.q: Does the speaking test affect my IGCSE grade?
a: It depends on your syllabus code. For 0510 and 0993, the Speaking Endorsement versions, the mark is reported separately on the certificate as a grade from 1 to 5 and does not contribute to the grade for the written components. For 0511 and 0991, the Count-in Speaking versions, it does count towards the overall grade.

items.q: Can I take notes during the preparation minute?
a: No. The syllabus states that candidates are not allowed to make any written notes during the preparation time for the short talk. You keep the card itself until the end of the talk, so plan in your head and use the card as your prompt.

items.q: Who marks the speaking test?
a: Your own teacher or examiner conducts and marks it, using the notes and criteria Cambridge supplies with the assessment cards. Cambridge International then externally moderates a sample of the recordings, which is why every test must be recorded in full.
